source.title: Measuring Generalization with Optimal Transport
source.authors: Ching-Yao Chuang; Youssef Mroueh; Kristjan H. Greenewald; A. Torralba; S. Jegelka

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports a label-corruption comparison relevant to V1, using Wide-ResNets and generalization error. It also evaluates different margin measures as predictors of generalization, but does not test the magnitude-aware sharpness named in V7.
record.gate_note: Section 5.2 trains one Wide-ResNet with true labels and one with random labels; both reach 100% training accuracy, with different reported generalization errors. Margin-distribution comparisons are shown in Figure 2, with textual descriptions but no numeric values. The PGDL scores and cited results are not rows because they do not report a direct test of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Section 5.2 repeats the original label-corruption comparison using its training code (Appendix B.5), measuring training accuracy and generalization error with Wide-ResNets on CIFAR-10.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately describes the label-corruption findings. The broader conclusion is that optimal-transport-based k-variance margin bounds predict generalization on PGDL and connect generalization with concentration and separation of learned features.
record.recipe_differences: Follows the label-corruption experiment setup in Zhang et al. (2017), training two Wide-ResNets and measuring generalization error; the paper adds margin-distribution analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Label condition changes the reported generalization error and margin-distribution distinction.

fits_no_version.finding: K-variance normalized margins distinguish natural-label and random-label models, whereas ordinary and gradient-normalized margins struggle.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature-distribution normalization can improve margin measures' ability to distinguish models with different generalization errors.

record.problems: The label-corruption comparison reports two models and no uncertainty estimates. Figure 2 provides no numeric margin values in the text. The study does not directly measure magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.rows_left_out: No additional direct label-corruption results reported beyond the rows extracted. PGDL benchmark scores compare predictors and are outside the claim versions; cited findings are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: Original architectures and ImageNet are not tested. Both conditions use Wide-ResNets and the original training code; exact architecture configurations and absence of explicit regularization are not documented in the supplied text.
No test-error trajectory across widths beyond interpolation.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected accuracy comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No held-out performance comparison across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness measurement or comparison of its ranking with norms and margins.
No removal and retraining comparison involving memorized examples.

record.verdict_notes: Using two separately trained models is appropriate for the label-assignment comparison; it does not itself imply different architectures or recipes. The study is not an original source for V1. Predictor benchmark scores do not test V7 merely because they concern generalization.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test Inception, AlexNet, MLPs, ImageNet, or the claim that the same architecture and recipe fit both label assignments; the comparison uses two Wide-ResNets.
The paper measures margin distributions and feature concentration, not magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
